title_en: Psychiatric examination of child and adolescent
place: A high-street opticians on a school-holiday Wednesday: a frame-display wall and a dispensing bench down one side, two test rooms with their doors hooked open, the lit letter chart at the far end of the test lane, and a low toy table beside the waiting chairs.
activity: Everyone is working through a sight test — reading a line off the chart with one eye covered under a paddle, following the pen-torch with their eyes, sitting up to the phoropter, trying a frame at the mirror while a parent answers the questions across the desk.
anchor_structure: The full-length test lane — the studded carpet strip with the back-lit letter chart standing at its far end and the facing mirror above it — running from the lower-left corner of the frame to the upper right, dividing the shop into waiting chairs, dispensing bench, test lane and the glazing workshop behind.
pun_explanation: M-S-E stands as an ordered subsequence of word-initials inside an utterly ordinary optician's fascia — the expreSS tRIps device — and it is planted in the one high-street trade whose examinees are children of every age with a parent sitting beside them, which is what the vehicle-test version could not supply. The trade then pays out on all five aspects with no invention: a sight test is run in a fixed non-negotiable order, history then acuity then cover test then refraction then the light, so examination structure is the venue's own procedure; the record card carries the child's whole history back to the first visit and the parent supplies it across the desk, so developmental history and parent interview are one piece of counter business; the method changes with age — pictures for the pre-schooler, letters for the schoolchild, a moving toy for the infant who cannot answer — which is the chapter's central teaching point rendered as ordinary shop routine; the optometrist down on the floor rolling a toy for a two-year-old to fix and follow is play observation as a real clinical technique rather than a metaphor; and because every examinee in the frame is an actual child, appearance, speech, mood and behaviour are all literal depiction. The chart's shrinking graded rows are a native developmental ladder and the red recall tabs standing proud of the record drawer are the red flags.

place: A small car-ferry terminal on the mainland side at midday: two identical passenger wings either side of the vehicle marshalling lanes, an enclosed footbridge crossing above them, a glazed control tower on the quay, the linkspan ramp down onto the ship, and the island lying out across the water.
activity: Everyone is catching the ferry — checking in at the booths, wheeling cases up the ramp, holding a boarding card out at the barrier, reading the departure board, edging cars forward in the marshalling lanes.
anchor_structure: The enclosed steel footbridge crossing over the marshalling lanes on a diagonal from the lower-left of the frame to the upper right, joining the two identical passenger wings, with the glazed control tower standing at its midpoint.
pun_explanation: The terminal's ordinary layout IS the gross anatomy, and the fascia spends its lettering on the one Latin morpheme that is already a brain region: insula means island, and the island is the destination painted on every board in the building. Two identical mirror-image wings joined by a single bridge = the hemispheres and the corpus callosum. The glazed control tower that every vessel and every vehicle must be routed through and which touches nothing else = thalamus as obligatory relay. The harbourmaster's office up over the concourse, watching the whole floor and overruling the lanes = prefrontal cortex. The marshalling lanes with their hold-and-release light = basal ganglia gating, and the turn-back bay for vehicles that joined the wrong queue = anterior cingulate conflict and error monitoring. The muster klaxon and the quay foghorn = amygdala. The bank of left-luggage lockers = hippocampus. The duty-free counter where everything is sniffed, priced and compared = orbitofrontal. The boiler-house thermostat and the canteen hatch = hypothalamus. The counterweighted linkspan trimmed continuously to hold the deck level with the quay = cerebellum. The lounge of people with three hours to kill, staring at nothing = the default mode network. Per the p272 rule no business pun is spent: one morpheme sits on a surface whose real job is bearing a name.

activity: Everyone is taking in the morning delivery — lifting crates down off the lorries at the kerb, wheeling sack-trucks in through the doorways, signing the docket on the driver's board, and carrying the empties back out to be loaded up again.
anchor_structure: The unbroken run of shopfront fascias with the kerb and gutter line beneath them, running from the lower left of the frame up to the colliery gates at the top right, splitting the picture into pavement, roadway, shopfronts and the upper windows above them.
pun_explanation: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger, and Messenger Row is an ordinary street nameplate that carries one morpheme of the everyday referent without printing the medical word — the same device the accepted transmitter reading used, and within the Lithium Lift precedent. This is the one chapter the spec says must not invent a venue: the seven course-wide premises are the content, so the plate is the street they stand on. A shop row is the only mundane container that holds a colliery, a hotel, a dairy, a club door, a weaving workshop, a seed merchant and a police box in one coherent frame at one light source. The delivery round then supplies the whole mechanism free: release is a crate carried in off the lorry, and reuptake is the same hand carrying the empties back out to be loaded again, which is a native action in the trade rather than a metaphor. Each premises signs for its own crate, so every messenger stays addressable at its own doorway instead of becoming one of seven nameplated boxes in a line-up.

pun_explanation: 5-H-T stands as an ordered subsequence of word-initials inside an entirely ordinary market name and street address — the expreSS tRIps device, and a numeral at the front of a market name is native signage rather than an intrusion. The hall was chosen because serotonin's whole story is one narrow midline workshop that ships everywhere, and a market's central aisle is literally its seam: the weaving stall stands on it and its goods go out to every other counter in the building. The receptor family then costs nothing, because each one is an ordinary trade already found in a market hall — a curtained fortune-teller's booth in the corner, the pie stall kitchen behind it, the wash-down channels of the fish end, the second-hand book stall, and the all-night kiosk in the corner arch. The postal collection at the delivery bay gives reuptake a native worker instead of a symbol.

pun_explanation: Nor'east is the compass reading NE spoken aloud and it is a perfectly ordinary way to name a family show — the corpus already owns the N-compass as the fixed glyph for this transmitter, so the fascia hooks straight onto a symbol the learner already holds. The showground was picked because it is the only mundane workplace that legitimately holds all three fixed structures at once in one light: a band on its own rostrum at the ring fence, a call box at the gate through which every message for the ground passes, and a snowy pine treeline with a pack standing out on the open ground beyond the ropes. It is a morning of work, not a performance, so the register stays flat and the strangeness sits in the props. The trade also pays out on the chapter's own mechanism without invention — everything on the ground is either hauled out on a rope or hauled back in on one, and one keeper stands at the fence with a dart rifle.

The rest of the syllabus falls out of the stock: the subtypes are two boats, one that takes nothing on at all and one that fills its tank and then runs the bilge pump straight back over the side; the gauge board and the boat-gauging tape are the assessment instruments and also the disturbed reading of a hull that plainly fits and is recorded as too wide; bradycardia is the paddle wound at half speed, hypothermia the cold green water, the low electrolytes three low marks on the same board, and osteopenia the crumbling mortar of the chamber wall, which is the only structural thing in the frame and is losing it. Family-based treatment is the strongest image the venue supplies: a family works one boat through with the parents on the paddle gear controlling the rate of filling and the adolescent aboard, which is exactly the transfer of control FBT prescribes. Mortality is carried by the lifebelt, the rescue pole and the plate on the wall, and by the fact that this is the only venue in the batch where the ordinary hazard is drowning.

title_en: Sleep development in children + adolescent shift
place: A small municipal observatory in a town park on a public open night: the dome with its slit rolled back over the lawn, a row of borrowed telescopes set out on the grass, the warm room with its log desk and clock board, and the park gate standing open onto the road.
activity: Everyone is observing: bending to an eyepiece and winding the focus, swinging a finder onto a target, holding a red torch over a chart, writing a line into the log book, and cranking the dome round a few degrees to keep up.
anchor_structure: The long white refractor tube on its cast-iron equatorial mount — pier, counterweight, tube and dew shield — running from the lower-left of the frame up and out through the open dome slit at the top right, splitting the scene into the dome floor, the warm room, the observing lawn and the park gate.
pun_explanation: Phase is the same word in both trades: an observatory's whole business is phase, and a delayed phase is the chapter. The name is therefore an exact homonym planted in a place name a real observatory would carry, and it prints no clinical word at all. The choice earns its keep because the venue owns, as ordinary equipment, the two objects that make the adolescent shift explicable rather than merely stated. First, two clocks hang on the same warm-room wall reading different times — sidereal and civil — because the sky keeps a period that is not twenty-four hours; that is the internal clock against the school clock, and the discrepancy is an instrument reading, not a mood. Second, the moonrise table pinned beside them lists a rise time roughly fifty minutes later on every successive line, so the picture contains a printed, native, undeniable object whose whole content is a clock that runs later every day. Nothing else in the course supplies that. Sleep architecture by age is literal depiction inside one shared activity: the smallest visitors swing their scopes all over the sky and never settle, which is REM-heavy infant sleep; the school-age children are the ones standing guard over the hour-long exposure that must not be jogged, which is slow-wave; the adults get short broken looks between clouds. Required hours by age become the booking board of session lengths, a properly numbered carrier. The venue is also open at night in a town, which is the only reason the fixed 24-hour store can stand across the road without contrivance — and the sixth-formers drifting out of the gate towards it while everyone else is packing up is the phase delay and its consequence in one movement.

place: A canal lock staircase on a busy summer morning: five stone chambers stepping up the hillside one straight into the next, black-and-white balance beams swung out over the towpath, a lock-keeper's hut with a toll window beside the bottom gate, a line of boats waiting their turn along the bank below, and side ponds and an overflow weir running down beside the flight.
activity: Everyone is working a boat up through the locks — winding a paddle up on a windlass, walking a balance beam open with their back against it, holding a rope round a bollard while the chamber fills, walking the boat forward into the next chamber.
anchor_structure: The flight of five chambers with its balance beams — a stepped run of stone walls and timber gates climbing the hillside — cutting the frame from the lower left to the upper right and dividing it into the waiting line below, the chambers themselves, the towpath and the keeper's hut.
pun_explanation: A staircase lock is the continuum of care built in stone. A boat is lifted one level at a time, no level can be skipped, it can only be taken up when the level above is ready to receive it, and it comes back down the same way it went up — which is the step-up and step-down criteria drawn as ordinary canal work rather than as a ladder diagram. Five chambers give the five settings in order from the open pound at the bottom, through the two shallow middle chambers, to the top chamber with the deepest walls and the gates shut behind it. The keeper is the case manager: he owns no boat, and decides only who enters, in what order, and how long each lies in the pound. Every remaining item is a real fitting on a real flight. Milieu is the posted routine on the hut wall — operating hours, the order of working, the rule that no boat enters alone. The token economy is literally a token economy, because tolls on the cut were paid in numbered brass checks and the keeper's board is hung with them. Restraint is the moment this chapter is careful about, and the flight makes it ordinary, brief and bounded: while the chamber is filling and the water is at its most turbulent the boat is held short on two ropes round the bollards, by two people, for exactly as long as the level is unsettled, and let go the moment it settles. Stop planks stacked against the wall are crisis containment; the bypass channel and the weir carry all the water that never needs a chamber at all, which is the least restrictive route; the side ponds hold what the flight cannot; and a boat coming back down past the waiting line is readmission.

title_en: Psychodynamic: Anna Freud, Klein, Kohut, Mentalization
place: A puppet-maker's workshop on the evening shift: a long carving bench of vices and glue pots down the middle, an overhead stringing rail above it hung with marionettes on control bars, a wall of shallow parts trays to the ceiling, a full-length rehearsal mirror at the far end and wood shavings underfoot.
activity: Everyone is making a puppet — carving and gluing at the bench, painting faces at the paint end, knotting strings up to the rail, and working a finished one by hand in front of the mirror.
anchor_structure: The long carving bench with the overhead stringing rail running above it, corner to corner from lower-left to upper-right down the whole depth of the room, splitting the frame into parts-tray wall / bench / stringing rail / mirror end.
pun_explanation: KLEIN is the theorist's surname used exactly as a maker's trade name is used, and for this audience it is also simply the word small — a workshop that makes small people. The workshop then pays the rest of the chapter out of its own furniture without inventing anything. Klein's part-objects are the shallow trays sorted by part: a tray of heads, a tray of hands, a tray of glass eyes, the object existing only in pieces; the depressive position is the mending bench where a snapped puppet is clamped and glued back into one whole thing, which is Klein's own word, reparation. Anna Freud's hierarchy of defences is the three-step drying rack, rough blanks at the bottom, varnished faces on top. Kohut's three selfobject needs are three ordinary workshop pairings: a maker holding a puppet up to the mirror, an apprentice under the tall maestro marionette hung highest on the rail, and two identical twins sharing one control bar. And mentalization is the trade itself — a hand up inside a hollow head, a fixed wooden face that has no mind of its own, and a second person who must read one into it and answer it.

place: A municipal public lending library on a wet afternoon: a long issue desk with a date-stamp block, a returns chute and its trolley, tall shelving bays running back into the room, a card-catalogue cabinet on the end wall and a low children's corner behind a half-gate.
activity: Everyone is borrowing and returning books — browsing the bays, carrying an armful to the desk to be date-stamped, emptying the returns trolley and shelving what came back.
anchor_structure: The long issue desk with the returns trolley run beside it and the tall shelving bays behind, running lower-left to upper-right across the room and splitting the frame into returns chute and entrance / issue desk / open bays / children's corner and closed stacks.
pun_explanation: A lending library is the only ordinary building whose entire trade is objects leaving their owner and coming back, which is what the chapter is about, and the sign carries the theorist's name the way every municipal library carries its donor's. The mapping is exact and free: object constancy is the card-catalogue drawer, where a card stands for a book that is not on the shelf and is not lost — the internal representation of an absent object, filed in alphabetical order. Mahler's whole sequence is the loan cycle: the toddler in the children's corner who carries one picture book out to a parent at the desk and straight back to the low shelf is practicing and refuelling; the RESERVED shelf behind the desk holds a named item until its owner comes, which is Winnicott's holding, and the taped, mended, much-borrowed picture book still in circulation is good-enough. The transitional object is that same book, refused at the desk by the child who brought it in. True and false self is the bright dust jacket over the drab cloth board underneath. Kernberg gets the returns desk: two triage trays, one to re-shelve and one to withdraw, with nothing allowed in between, and a trolley of spine-labelless books that belong to no section at all.

title_en: Later theorists: Erikson, Bion, Ogden, Lacan, Spitz, Stern, relational
place: A bellhanging works on a fitting-out day: the trial frame standing down the middle of the shed with a graded ring of eight bells bolted into it, wheels and headstocks laid out on the boards beneath, a vertical tuning lathe at one end with a bell mouth-up under the cutter, an inspection and lettering bench along the window wall, and the ropes dropping through the floor holes into the pit below.
activity: Everyone is fitting out and sounding bells — bolting a bell onto its headstock, hanging its wheel and rope, cutting metal off one on the tuning lathe, and striking each bell with a hand hammer to hear it.
anchor_structure: The timber-and-steel trial frame carrying the ring of eight bells, running from the lathe end at lower left up to the yard doors at upper right, the largest thing in the shed, splitting the frame into the tuning lathe and its swarf / the eight bells in the frame / the lettering and inspection bench along the windows / the rope pit and the open yard doors.
pun_explanation: A bell is a hollow container whose entire job is to take a raw meaningless blow from a clapper held inside it and hand it back as a note — Bion's container-contained and alpha-function are the physical operation of the trade, so the works carries his name on its board the way the corpus lets a barbershop carry barbiturates. Everything else the chapter tests is then ordinary bellhanging stock. A ring is eight bells graded by size, numbered on their headstocks and rung strictly from treble to tenor with no bell skipped, which is Erikson's fixed epigenetic sequence; the one bell whose inscription band is still blank, with its loose letters spilled across the bench, is identity versus role confusion. A bell sounds five partials at once and none of them replaces the one below it — Stern's layered senses of self — and the tuner brings them in by striking a fork, laying his palm flat on the metal and cutting until fork and bell agree, which is affect attunement working across two senses at once; the instant two bells strike dead together is the moment of meeting, and the beat tone two mistuned bells make, belonging to neither of them, is Ogden's analytic third, while the hand run slowly over the polished soundbow feeling for a flaw is the autistic-contiguous surface. The bright band on that soundbow gives a whole curved figure back to whoever leans over it, which is Lacan's mirror stage, and one bell carries his three orders as three bands: the reflecting one, the cast inscription of raised letters, and the rough unmachined crown nobody finishes. The dull green bell standing unhung in the corner with its clapper hanging on a nail is Spitz's hospitalism; a bell puts its whole weight on the headstock it leans on, so the one lying on its side with the headstock off is the anaclitic case; and the muffle box gives protest, despair and detachment as one bell open, one half-muffled and one with its clapper tied. Every rope drops through the same floor holes into one pit, so two crossed ropes pulling two men off balance, neither of them having meant it, is the two-person field and the enactment.

title_en: Telemental health for children and adolescents
place: A model flying club's field on a bright Sunday morning: a mown grass strip with a white-painted flight line along it, marked pilot boxes on the grass, a row of pits bays behind with models on trestles, a timber clubhouse with a peg board by its door, and a boundary hedge with the far side of the valley beyond it.

pun_explanation: Tele- is the chapter's own first morpheme and it means at a distance, so a club whose field is called Telescope Hill reads as a genuine club name, keeps the morpheme, and says far-seeing without printing the topic. The whole hobby is the chapter's literal picture: the pilot never touches the thing he is responsible for, works entirely by watching a small figure play at a distance, and everything can go wrong at the far end of a link. Every fact then hangs on ordinary field furniture. The peg board by the hut door, where you must take your channel's peg before switching on or two sets clash and both models come down, is the shared insecure channel, and the bind plug taped inside one transmitter is the paired encrypted link. The buddy-box lead joining an instructor's set to a beginner's, so the adult can take control on the instant, is the parent in the room and the supervising clinician on the line at once. The canvas windbreak screening one pits bay is the private space the child is entitled to, and the spotter standing at a pilot's shoulder is the second pair of eyes the remote observer does not have. The laminated card wired to the gate giving the field's exact location, beside the pinned emergency plan and the first-aid box, is the rule that you establish where the patient physically is before the session starts; the owner's name-and-address label in an open fuselage hatch, the failsafe setting and the lost-model alarm beeping out in the long grass beyond the hedge are what you do once the link is already gone, and the retrieval barrow is the fetch. The thirty-pace range-check stake is the technology check before you begin. The boundary hedge and its line of posts, which no model may be flown across, is licensure and jurisdiction, and the affiliation certificate screwed up in the hut is the licence itself. The proficiency-certificate board with names and dates on it is the evidence base, the signing-in book and the clipboard of forms are consent, and the laptop running a simulator on the trestle table inside the hut is the app used between sessions and never instead of them.

place: An assay office on a busy trade morning: a long testing bench down the middle with a rack of acid bottles and a row of beam balances, a black touchstone slab at the near end, a hallmark punch press at the far end, and a brass-grilled trade counter where jewellers hand in numbered trays.

The office then hands over its stock as free fact slots. The fineness chart on the wall is a ladder of grades from coarsest to purest, which is the hierarchy of evidence with the top grade at the top. The acid bottles are the test that either holds or does not. The one joke the venue tells for free is the ring mandrel, where an adult ring is being cut down to fit a child's finger and re-tested.
